blurb: The closure given to `parForEach`, `parTraverse`, `parTraverseAll` or `parTraverseTry` (or their `…With` forms) runs once per element, all at once, so it may not write a `store` field, which is the rule a `par { … }` block already follows. Every `<-` is an await point, so a `get` then a `put` in the closure lets the other branches write in between, and their updates are lost. A single call such as `update` is atomic per key, but it is refused here too, so the two rules stay equal. Run the loop with `forEach` (or `traverseAll` / `traverseTry`), where each element finishes before the next starts, so a single-call `update` stays atomic. A store write reads the entry before it stages the write, so the sequential form reads one entry at a time; per-key atomicity is the reason for the rule. To keep the concurrent part, collect with `parTraverseAll` and write afterwards.
summary: A closure passed to `parForEach`, `parTraverse`, `parTraverseAll` or `parTraverseTry` writes a `store` field (`put`, `remove`, `update`, `upsert`, `add`, `append` or `:=`). Its branches run concurrently, and a `get` then a `put` across them loses updates, so store writes stay sequential, as they do in a `par { … }` block.
